blocks.1: There are many ideas about how the village got its name. In the local history of Gulen, published in 1973, Ivar Kleiva writes that one can meet older people who pronounce the name “øi’nnjevik”. This can be compared with what Dean Dahl mentions in an article in “Budstikken” in 1824, where he says he has heard that the name is supposed to be “Ønevig” or “Eyarvig” (the bay that is sheltered by, or lies in the lee of, islands). Among other things, Dahl says: “Indeed the common people also pronounce it Ønevig, and not Evindvig”.
blocks.2: The ways I have seen the name written are: Øyuindarviik, Øyfindarvik, Æyvindarviik, Ewyndeveyck, Evendvijg, Evindvig, Evenvik, Eivinvik and Eivindvik. On an old map I have also seen Edvindvik.
blocks.3: Some believe the name may have developed from Eidvin, which would mean “the plain where they swore the oath”. E. Bjordø, who has written a good deal about the church and the place here, gives Eidvin translated as Tingvoll (“assembly field”). Albert Joleik writes the same in an article in “Syn og Segn” for December 1917. He also mentions the name forms “Eidvinjarvik” and “Eivindarvik”. He says that the form Eivinvik agrees with what people say now (1917): “no one says the name with a d, except when they read it”. He goes on: “Ei(d)vinvik = Tingvoll-vaag” (assembly-field bay).
blocks.4: Some also claim that the place is named after a well-known person called Eivind/Øyvind or similar. If that is the case, I believe, like most who have written about this, that the place earlier had another name with a natural connection to the area.
blocks.5: Dahl believes that the mighty old Gaulom had its main seat here, with its “agiæta høfut-hof” (splendid chief temple), placed in the area where the church now stands. Several others agree with him that the people of a large area had their gathering place and their sanctuaries here far back in heathen times too. Dahl evidently researched this thoroughly, and in addition to the article in “Budstikken” in 1824 mentioned above, he takes up the subject in an article reprinted in “Det kgl. norsk videnskabers selskaps skrifter i det 19. årh., III, pp. 77–98” (1826), and as usual he is thorough. In both articles he tries to prove that Gaulom must have been in Gulen, and he believes the Gulating stood on the site of old Gaulom. He believes the name Gaulom comes from gavl, which means an “end, side, bottom or bay of something”, and says that “the plural of Gavel is undoubtedly Gavlom or Gaulom in the Norwegian language; for u and v were and still are used interchangeably as letters of the same meaning; so when it is used of a whole community, it means several ends or bays of fjords reaching more or less far into the land”.
blocks.6: In the article of 1826 he writes that “Gaul” is still used in everyday speech in Nordhordland of a “bay or arm of the sea”, and “Paul” of an inlet that runs dry at low tide. He tries to show how well Gulen, compared with what we see in the sagas and legends, fits the historical Gaulom. He believes that Gaular in Sunnfjord is named after the river Gaula, which in turn got its name from the sound (the roaring) of the river. I have the impression that this is also the view of people in Gaular. It is now also generally accepted that the Gulating must have been in Gulen (south of the Sognefjord, in what was then Nordhordland) and not in Gaular (north of the Sognefjord). Perhaps this is partly a result of Dahl's thorough work. Dahl believes that the Gulating and old Gaulom were in one and the same place, and that they were not at Osen in Sunnfjord but in Gulen. I find what he writes very interesting, with many good arguments and sensible conclusions, but it would take far too long to repeat it all here.
blocks.7: In the local history of Gulen, Ivar Kleiva writes that “Eivindvik was originally a true large farm. It reached from Dingja in the north-west, owned the land on the east side of Folefotsundet, the north side of Prestesundet, and all around Midtunvågen to Merkesvika towards Floli. The farm had vast mountain areas to the north and east, and the islands as well: Vesøy, Fonna and Tyløy (Marøy or Napsøy), many thousands of decares in all.”
blocks.8: Dahl also believes there was a large farm here. He thinks it likely that all the farms from the parsonage to Floli, and likewise all “farms from Skjerjehavn and around Evindvig parsonage on all sides within a distance of ¾ mile, have been, if not a single farm, then almost one estate; at the very least nowhere else is so much land held by the Church, the clergy and charitable foundations gathered in one place as here”.
blocks.10: The map from 1771 shows parts of the old parish of Evenvig.
blocks.11: Several historians have suggested that large landholdings were connected with Eivindvik. Professor Knut Robberstad, for example, writes in a paper on the Gulating that the living here had “plenty of landed property”. A number of the farms in Gulen were church property. Lieutenant Colonel Holck writes in an article in “Budstikken” in 1824, among other things: “the farm Floelie as well as the quite handsome farms lying between it and Evenvig parsonage, namely Underthun, Midthun, Henriksbøe, Gryten etc., are all either benefices or church property, and so have probably in the past formed a common property at the disposal of the state”. Dahl has suggested that the area may have been a kind of common land, and the words “at the disposal of the state” may point to the same thing. It seems that those who have written about this believe that Eivindvik was the centre of this large property.
blocks.12: We know nothing certain about what the name of the property may have been. Dahl believes, as mentioned, that this was the site of the old, well-known gathering and sacrificial place Gaulom. In an article in “Urda”, A. Brømel holds that when Olav Tryggvason had Christianity adopted at the Gulating in 997, “the old idol temple which stood at Gaulom was also torn down, the idols destroyed, the ancient venerable oak trunks of the sacred grove cut down, and first a stone cross raised, and later a Christian church built and consecrated where a heathen temple had stood before.” So it seems that Brømel agrees with Dahl here. Could it be that the name Gaulom became Guli/Gula? Several people have claimed so.
blocks.13: Ludvig Holm-Olsen has also discussed the name Eivindvik. In an article in “Bergens Tidende” on 5–6 July 1966 he writes, among other things: “The large farm in Eivindvik has hardly had this name from the beginning. Perhaps the name of the fjord, Guli, became the name of a farm by the bay here at the fjord, and later of the whole area.”
blocks.14: In the paper by Knut Robberstad mentioned above, he suggests, as one of several alternatives, that Guløy could be the name of the old farm of which Midtun, Henriksbø and Undertun are parts, or it may have been an older name for Eivindvik. As we know, and as Robberstad also mentions, the word øy did not only mean land surrounded by water; it could also be flat, perhaps gently sloping, land lying by a lake or the sea. Examples of this use of øy in names are Ringøy and Vikøy in Hardanger, Fossøy in Jostedal and many more.
blocks.15: Another name I have heard mentioned as a possible name for the place around the church here is Ve. Vesøyna, which belonged to the parsonage and is still public property, is explained as the island belonging to Ve. In Old Norse, ve meant “sanctuary”, and it goes back to the people having their sanctuary here in heathen times too.
blocks.16: In Dean Dahl's article in “Budstikken” in 1824 he mentions the tradition that there was once a monastery in Eivindvik. He thinks the name of the place may have been changed so that it was named after a well-known clergyman, monk or priest. There are many examples of place names changing over time. They may have been renamed after people, after events, and for other, perhaps more or less accidental, reasons, and the old names have fallen out of use and been forgotten. It is natural that when the large property that may have had its centre here was split up, each of the separated holdings got its own name. If we look at the farms in Midtunvågen, it seems reasonable that Midtun, for example, was the farmyard (tun) in the middle, between Gryta (Grøtun) and Henriksbø. Henriksbø was probably called something else then, perhaps “Myra” (the bog). Kleiva writes about this in the local history and says that “the very form of the name Myra suggests that the farm was split off from a larger unit.” He also writes that the name Henriksbø was probably not in use before around 1500.
blocks.17: It is claimed that in really old times Gryta was part of Midtun. Perhaps that is why the bay leading in towards Gryta is called Midtunvågen. The road between the area by the church and the farms in Midtunvågen used to run through Grytelia. Perhaps it continued across the Midtun river to an “Øvstun” (upper farmyard) at the head of the bay, which in later times became Henriksbø?
blocks.18: Dahl writes that the names “Grytten or Grøthun, Midtun and Underthun, on the other hand, clearly reveal the moving out of houses on one and the same farm, since it is still customary to call the group of houses belonging to each holding on one and the same farm a Thun.” So here he finds yet another argument that these farms were all split off from the earlier large farm. That sounds very likely.
blocks.19: The bay out here, at the mouth of the ravine, sheltered and fertile, protected by islands and mountains, was surely well placed as a possible main seat of a larger unit. It must have been a very suitable place for the saga people's gatherings, sanctuaries and ceremonies. Perhaps the place was quite simply called Gjøli at first, from the Old Norse “gjøl”, meaning ravine or cleft. Gjøli may have developed into Guli, which people coming from outside to the ceremonies here used as a name for the whole area. As the local names came more to the fore and were used more, also by outsiders, the gathering place itself was called by what it had then become – the plain or field where they swore the oath. This name may then have become established as the name of the centre of the area that was still called Guli. Associate Professor Linge also mentions that the name Guli may perhaps have developed from the Turkic word “kul” = human being.
blocks.20: Another word I would like to mention here is the Old Norse “gjø”, which in old times was used for the period that mainly covers what we now count as the first month of spring, March. The word is said to come from the vegetation spirit Gjø, which was a symbol of fertility. The spirit was probably also worshipped here at the gjøblot (goiblot, a spring sacrifice) in the hope of fruitful gatherings and fruitful years. Could this have had some bearing on the name of an area where important gatherings met in the spring?
blocks.21: When the system of parishes was introduced, the parish was named after its main seat here. It would therefore be natural to believe that the place already at that time had the name that has developed into what is now written Eivindvik. I have read that this parish is probably one of the oldest, and in its day perhaps also one of the largest, parishes in the country.
blocks.22: Per Linge, formerly associate professor at Østfold University College, and his wife Britt were here in Eivindvik twice in the summer of 2007. Linge had much of interest to tell from history, comparing Turkic and Roman history with our own, including what we have from Snorri, and he believed that it was in the heyday of the Turks/Huns that Eivindvik began and developed as a historic site, according to Turkic rules and guidelines. He called the place a city under a Turkic system of government with legislative power, by far the oldest capital in Scandinavia. Much suggests that senators/priests lived here, and he believes the name may have developed from the Turkic word “Ayin” (there should be a ^ over the letter A here), which comes from ceremony or ritual, to Ayvin-vik. He also points to the word “ayru”, which actually means equal in rank, and “denk”, which can mean “ting” (in the sense of an assembly, a seat of assembly).
blocks.23: Eivindvik has become part of the research project Linge is now working on, which is intended to be published as a book, something we look forward to with excitement.
